newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico seen ready to bail out toll-road operators.
newsitem.headline: Mexico seen ready to bail out toll-road operators.

text.p: The Mexican government appears set to retake control of most of the country's toll highways in an effort to clean up one of the last remaining messes linked to the 1994-95 economic crisis, analysts said.

The government is expected to pay several billion dollars to buy back either all or part of some 3,750 miles of highways privatized during former President Carlos Salinas's 1988-1994 administration. The road projects became unviable when the peso's devaluation led to surging interest rates and plunging consumer demand.

Financial markets and private companies interested in bidding for future Mexican privatizations such as railroads, ports and electricity projects will watch the outcome closely to see how the government deals with concessions gone awry.

"The most important thing is to see how the government handles it, so it sets a precedent for other concession companies to deal with the government when privatization does not pan out," Sobani Warner, an analyst at Bear, Stearns in New York, told Reuters.

Having already spent billions helping banks clean up their balance sheets and having pushed through costly tax relief for businesses and consumers, the government has yet to find an acceptable solution to the road privatizations.

Mexican newspaper Reforma said on Tuesday the government could unveil a toll-road rescue plan later in the day after more than two years of negotiations between private road operators and the government.
And newspaper La Cronica on Monday said the government had agreed to spend between 25 and 30 billion pesos on the bailout plan. This year's budget earmarked some $3.3 billion for the rescue project.

Toll road projects, already losing money before the peso crash, went into default soon afterwards, as interest rates skyrocketed and made financing the projects virtually impossible. At the same time, revenues plunged because of the recession, with drivers balking at expensive tolls.

"The result was a disaster -- losses for the private builders, past-due debt for banks, the majority of private highways turned into white elephants, too much traffic on state-run highways," Mexico City daily La Cronica said in an editorial on Monday.

The dream road projects became a nightmare for companies such as Empresas ICA, Grupo Tribasa and Grupo Mexicano de Desarrollo, which paid dearly for the concessions. ICA alone has some $1.3 billion in toll roads on its books, analysts say.

Analysts said they expected the government to buy back the highways at a big discount, probably at 40 to 50 cents in the dollar. But almost nothing is known about the plan's details, including whether the government will take full control of the highways or how it will pay for its stake.
"It is the framework of the deal that is at question. There are a thousand more questions than answers," Warner said.
At this point, the most important thing may be to finish the deal so that construction companies can get back on track and start on other badly needed projects, analysts say.
For its part, the government has earmarked some eight billion pesos over the next three years for building roads on its own, without the private sector.
"What is bad at this point is the uncertainty," said Ben Uglow, an analyst at Robert Flemings in New York.
